noi_dung:
Using Electrotherapy to Purify the Air

The Chan Dharma-door is the dharma of directly pointing at people's minds, seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha; it is also the Sudden Teaching. The Sudden Teaching comes about through diligent cultivation of the Gradual Teaching. Hence the saying:

"Though the principle is suddenly awakened to, practice is cultivated gradually."

(Though the meaning may be understood in an instant, practice must proceed step by step.)

Right now, walking, standing, lying down, and sitting are all gradual practice. Wait until some day you truly understand, and you will suddenly become enlightened. That is "sudden." In fact, "sudden" is inseparable from "gradual"; "gradual" is precisely what aids "sudden."

Usually, cultivators each claim the dharma they practice is the finest, number one. If it were not number one, they would be unhappy, and they would refuse to cultivate. If you truly understood, then all dharmas are the Buddhadharma and all are unattainable (ungraspable); hence there is nothing worth clinging to.

Chan is a way of harmonizing body and mind. "Harmonizing the body" means keeping the body from agitation. "Harmonizing the mind" means keeping the mind from giving rise to discursive thoughts, ever pure. Once the mind is pure, all of empty space and the entire Dharma Realm lie within your own nature. Your own nature contains all things, embraces all things, and is precisely our Buddha-nature of old.

From limitless kalpas until now, life after life, we have been so deeply tainted by wrong views that it is not easy to understand the mind and see the nature. For this reason we "join a Chan Session." "Joining a Session" is called "setting a fixed period to win realization"—that is, fixing a definite time and a definite course for applying effort, seeking to attain penetrating clarity.

If you wish to truly penetrate and understand, first you must learn to act as if you knew nothing at all. In the Chan Hall, in applying effort, what method do you use? The method of "not knowing"—above, not knowing there is sky; below, not knowing there is earth; in between, not knowing there are people. From morning to night, what are you doing? Don't know! What food are you eating? Don't know! What clothes are you wearing? Don't know! As if in a stupor, knowing nothing at all. There is a saying:

Nurture great clumsiness, and only then is there skill;

Learn to be as a fool, and only then is wonder seen.

That is, if you can become like the stupidest person in the world, only then will marvelous skill arise. At that point:

Penetrate one, and penetrate them all;

Understand one, and understand them all;

Awaken to one, and awaken to them all.

(Penetrate one thing, and penetrate all things.

Clarify one thing, and clarify all things.

Awaken to one thing, and awaken to all things.)

Then you will penetrate all things and become thoroughly enlightened. What have you learned? Don't know—just like a fool. Yet right then, wonders appear.

When joining a Chan Session, you must set aside petty cleverness and sly shrewdness. Do not suppose you know and understand everything. To suppose you know everything is not true understanding of the Buddhadharma. There is a saying:

"Great wisdom appears as folly."

(One of great wisdom looks as if dull-witted.)

Outwardly they seem to understand nothing, yet in fact they understand everything. That is called "hazy on small matters, clear on great ones." Whoever is like that is one of great accomplishment.

In the Chan Hall, when the assembly runs, we run; when the assembly sits, we sit—east, west, south, north, we need not know. Then we will truly understand, truly comprehend. Understand what? Understand the "scenery of our homeland." Comprehend what? Comprehend our own "original face."

In the Chan Hall, apply effort in cultivation, speak fewer useless words, and waste no time.

"An inch of time is an inch of gold,

But an inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time."

Sitting in Chan is truly most precious. No one knows in which minute or second you will become enlightened, so seize every minute and second and let none slip by. If you go to the restroom, return to the Chan Hall at once and keep sitting. At the dining hall, finish eating and return to the Chan Hall at once; finish your tea and return to the Chan Hall at once. In short, do not miss your chance at enlightenment, for no one knows when that moment will be. In other words, circling, running, or sitting in Chan are all fine chances for enlightenment—let none slip by.

In the Qing dynasty, Emperor Yongzheng once invited Abbot Tianhui of Gaomin Monastery to Beijing to discuss the principles of Chan. The emperor asked whether he knew the tenet of National Master Yulin, and he could not answer. The emperor then ordered him to remain in the Chan Hall and find the answer within seven days, or lose his head. For six days he could not find the answer. On the last day, in extreme urgency, he ran round and round the Chan Hall. Running back and forth made him dizzy, and he crashed headlong into a pillar, raising a bump on his head! In that very instant his mind turned suddenly bright, and he found the answer. He then went to see the emperor. Emperor Yongzheng knew he had grasped National Master Yulin's tenet. From then on began the custom of circling (running incense) in the Chan Hall.

The Chan Hall has walking incense, running incense, sitting incense, and investigating the hua-tou. Walking incense means stepping briskly. Running incense means jogging slowly. Sitting incense means sitting in Chan. Investigating the hua-tou means turning a question over in the mind—as in investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" Wholeheartedly investigating that phrase, investigating to the point of single-minded unity, unstained by a single mote of dust—that is the moment of enlightenment. These are all methods to prevent and halt discursive thoughts. Only without discursive thoughts can there be awakening. The purpose of sitting in Chan is enlightenment. After enlightenment comes transcendental wisdom.

Thus the Patriarchs studied the method of "using poison to counter poison," using the investigation of the hua-tou to control discursive thoughts—that is, using one question to control all other questions. What hua-tou to investigate? Investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" When you find out "who," when you thoroughly understand "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?"—only then do you truly penetrate. Penetrate what? Penetrate the need to stay far from all that is upside down and contentious.

The Heart Sutra teaches:

"Far apart from upside-down dream-like thinking, and reach Ultimate Nirvana."

This process requires a bout of bitter effort to succeed. If I speak too much, I will interrupt your skill. Best that you follow the rules, and truly apply effort in cultivation.

One thing you must understand is that in the "Three Character Classic" there is a line:

"What is precious is concentration."

(What is precious is singleness of purpose.)

Whatever you do, if you can focus wholeheartedly, the outcome will be success. Likewise, when investigating the hua-tou, think only of that one phrase—think of it morning and evening, while eating and sleeping, while walking and sitting; until you have pondered it to the point where "seas run dry and rocks split open," never give up. In other words, "unenlightened, never rest." Thinking of a single question alone is the truth; thinking of too many questions is discursive thought.

Two lines of verse are truly full of meaning:

If one sits still for but a brief moment,

It surpasses building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands.

(If one sits in stillness for a single instant,

It exceeds building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands.)

That describes the merit of sitting in Chan: if a meditator can still the mind for even a short while, that merit exceeds manyfold the merit of building stupas—as many as the Ganges' sands—of seven jewels. For raising countless stupas is at most an offering to the Buddha's sharira; but sitting still for an instant can fashion the Buddha's true body. Hence sitting still for an instant surpasses building many seven-jeweled stupas.

If sitting still for a moment holds such merit, then sitting day after day holds merit beyond reckoning. If in a brief span you give rise to no discursive thoughts and the mind is pure, gradually you will become "limpid and ever still."

Sitting still in the Chan Hall, your merit is not only limitless—for all humankind, that merit is also limitless. Someone asks: "How can my merit be shared with humankind, with the whole world?" People of today's world, scrambling for fame and gain, create a soaring murderous aura—selfish and self-serving, each scheming against the other—turning the world dark and gloomy, filled with poison. Humankind's strife grows ever fiercer, ever more dangerous, ever graver. If we find no way to rescue the world from the crisis enveloping it, surely one day the earth will explode! Why explode? Because science is now so advanced that the great powers are researching ever swifter weapons of murder, racing to build nuclear arms, laser beams, and the like.

Once war breaks out, such weapons will turn the earth to ashes. That will truly be humankind's last day.

Applying effort in cultivation in the Chan Hall, invisibly we can destroy that murderous aura and spare the world its crisis. How to destroy it? The air has been polluted by poisons, and directly or indirectly those poisons affect the health of beings, threatening the lives of all. Just look: nowadays strange illnesses grow ever more numerous, leaving doctors helpless. That is because the air is polluted, no longer fresh and clean—everywhere nothing but poison. We who cultivate the Way must use a kind of electrotherapy to dissolve the poisons in the air. What is "electrotherapy"? It is sitting still, from which the light of wisdom radiates. This light of wisdom is precisely an electric current. That current travels through space and detoxifies, turning turbid air into pure air. That is called healing the world's ills by electrotherapy.

Now someone doubts whether this principle is feasible: "How can sitting still dissolve poisons in the air?" Let me tell a story: in the Song dynasty there was a great man of letters named Su Dongpo. At that time there was also a Chan Master named Fo Yin. The two were friends in the Way, often visiting each other, as shown by this couplet testifying to their close friendship:

Coming and going, the monk is always Fo Yin.

Back and forth, no guest but Dongpo.

(Going out or in: Master Fo Yin is ever near.

To and fro: if not Dongpo's company, whose else?)

Once Su Dongpo composed a verse:

I bow my head to the God among gods;

His light shines upon the great chiliocosm.

The eight winds cannot move him;

Seated upright upon the purple-golden lotus.

(I bow to the God among gods (that is, the Buddha);

His light shines upon the universe.

The eight winds blow him not;

Firmly seated on the golden lotus throne.)

Su Dongpo sent it to Chan Master Fo Yin for comment, and the two fell into dispute over it. Now let us take the line "His light shines upon the universe" to illustrate a principle. This light is precisely electrotherapy, shining upon the entire great chiliocosm and dissolving its poisons. This light can dispel the turbid air of the universe, cleansing it utterly until not a trace of poison remains.

If you can radiate light shining throughout the universe, then your share of poison will dissolve. If others can radiate light shining throughout the universe, then their share of poison will be dispelled. If everyone can radiate light shining throughout the universe, then everyone's poison will be dissolved.

If all people join hearts and forces, using electrotherapy to heal the world's ills, then polluted air will steadily lessen and fresh air will steadily increase. Gradually the atmosphere will become wholly pure. Know that turbid air is poison, while fresh air is wisdom.

Why is the air polluted today? Because most people do not know how to cultivate, do not know how to use electrotherapy, so the air grows ever more turbid. We who cultivate the Way must take up the duty of making the air pure. Not only must we ourselves vigorously cultivate Chan, we must also encourage friends and kin to sit in Chan. The merit of sitting in Chan is limitless, with inconceivable benefit for body and mind. If they do not believe, tell them to try the experiment—sooner or later they will gain inconceivable benefit. Strive in sitting Chan. When your light shines throughout the great chiliocosm, the poisons in the air will naturally all be destroyed.

Take heed! You need only halt discursive thoughts, and you can radiate the light of wisdom. This light can shine throughout the great chiliocosm and purge the poisons in the air. You will reap limitless merit benefiting all humankind. What benefit? The power to dissolve the poisons polluting the air, so humankind no longer suffers calamity from grave illnesses. That is precisely indirect benefit to everyone.
